title: Knowing without fixing
hookLine: you know an angry mind as angry: that is the whole instruction

lines: AN INSTRUCTION HIDING IN PLAIN SIGHT.
cards: You notice you're anxious. Right away, a whole repair crew shows up. You should calm down.
Why are you like this? Try breathing slower. Think positive.
Fix it, fix it, fix it. And somehow the anxiety gets worse, now with frustration on top: anxious, and anxious about being anxious.
Yesterday's list in the sutta had an instruction hiding in it, so simple it's easy to miss.

teach.h: A MIND WITH ANGER: KNOW IT.
teach.b: Look again at the wording. A mind with anger: know it as a mind with anger. That's all.
It doesn't say, then remove the anger. It doesn't say, replace it with kindness. It doesn't say, feel bad for being angry.
In this section, the whole instruction is to know. Other teachings in the Buddhist tradition do give remedies, kindness for ill will, reflection on the body for lust, and those come later.
But the Satipatthana Sutta puts something first: before you change anything, see it clearly. Why?
Trying to fix a mind state usually means pushing against it, and pushing is its own kind of aversion. It's the second arrow again, aimed at your own moods. Knowing takes a step back.
Say, this is an angry mind, and there's no longer just anger. There's also a knowing of the anger.
There's a little space there, and in that space the anger can loosen by itself, the way a knot loosens when you stop pulling both ends. Look back over this week and the same move is everywhere.
The parts of the body, sorted like grain. The elements, felt as they are. The charnel ground: this body too.
Feelings: pleasant, painful, neither. The second arrow, not fired. The mind, known as the weather.
Every one of them is seeing, not fixing.

how: Insight meditation teachers often stress bare knowing of mind states, noting 'angry' or 'restless' without judgment, as the first step; remedies such as loving-kindness are taught separately.

o: working out what caused a mood, then fixing it
holding a fact in memory, sure that it's true
seeing a state clearly, without trying to fix it

games.q: match each day this week to its move.
p: sorted like a bag of grain

s: the sutta says to replace anger with kindness in this section
here the instruction is only to know it; remedies come from other teachings.
trying to fix a mood can become its own kind of pushing
a second arrow aimed at our own moods.
knowing a state can create a little space around it
there's the anger, and there's also the knowing of it.

games.q: you sit to meditate and notice you're irritated. what does the sutta's instruction on the mind say to do first?
o: know it: this is an irritated mind.
stop meditating until the mood passes.
games.why: the sutta says to know the mind as it is. seeing clearly comes before any change.

practice: Find whatever mood is here right now, restless, flat, content, tired, a little sad, and name it plainly: a restless mind. Instead of fixing it, stay with it the way you'd sit with a friend who doesn't need advice.
If the urge to fix shows up, know that too, a mind that wants to fix: nothing to do but know.

wordCard.voice: Knowing. In this section of the sutta, the whole instruction for a mind state, angry or calm, is simply to know it, nothing more.

carryVoice: Your line: just know it. Seeing comes before changing. Another week in the sutta, done.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikāya 10 (Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta), contemplation of mind
